(NASDAQ: FFAI) ("Faraday Future," "FF," or the "Company"), a California-based global Embodied AI ("EAI") ecosystem company, today announced that this week's Investor Weekly Report from FF Founder and Global CEO YT Jia has been rescheduled to October 14.

FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, featuring FF Nova, FF Nova Mini, the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0, and the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform.

FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0. (NASDAQ: FFR ) is a U.S.-based Embodied AI (EAI) robotics company that is in the process of acquiring the FF EAI Robotics business. Upon completion of the acquisition, the Company will focus on the research and development, manufacturing, commercialization, and deployment of intelligent robotic technologies, products, and industry solutions. The Company is committed to building a "Four-Core Full-Stack" AI ecosystem covering the full lifecycle of robotics, consisting of EAI Brain & Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory. Guided by the technology and product philosophy of "One Brain, Multi-forms, Multi-capabilities," the Company aims to empower humanoid, biomimetic, and other robotic form factors through a unified EAI Brain, while continuously expanding their multi-task and multi-scenario capabilities. The ecosystem is designed to support the full robotics lifecycle, including R&D, deployment, data collection and training, operations, and commercial applications. The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. The Company also operates RoboShare, a robot-sharing and services platform designed to connect robotic assets, service capabilities, customer demand, and ecosystem partners, further strengthening its robotics commercialization and service ecosystem. LOS ANGELES--( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc. (NASDAQ: FFAI) (“Faraday Future,” “FF,” or the “Company”), a California-based global Embodied AI (“EAI”) ecosystem company, today announced that it has signed definitive agreements with FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR) (renamed from AIxCrypto Holdings, Inc. and AIXC) for FFR to acquire FFAI’s full robotics ecosystem business at an agreed valuation of approximately $200 million. The transaction advances the parties’ previously announced transaction process to the definitive agreement stage. Its structure has been simplified to facilitate execution and closing. Following closing, FFR will become the first U.S.-listed pure-play “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” humanoid and bionic EAI robotics ecosystem company, with the goal of maintaining a top three overall ranking in the EAI robotics industry over the next five years. FFAI plans to adopt an upgraded operating model inspired by Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet and upgrade from EAI vehicle manufacturing to a Robotaxi Sharing Network and AI VisiCabin technology operator, joining forces with RoboShare to build a lighter-asset shared mobility model. Following the strategic upgrade, FFAI plans to work with RoboShare to expand shared mobility, Robotaxi and EAI cabin businesses; explore integrating FF’s “3rd aiSpace” (Intelligent Cabin) into shared vehicles; and facilitate the connection of FFAI vehicles to the Robotaxi network. These efforts are intended to create synergies among vehicles, cabin experiences, and shared operations. By leveraging RoboShare’s sharing platform and operational capabilities, FFAI also plans to pursue opportunities in vehicle-asset onboarding, operations and user services. Share Issuance at $2.246 per Share, a Premium to FFR’s Market Price Under the definitive agreements, the parties agreed on a valuation of approximately $200 million for FFAI’s robotics business and approximately $60 million for FFR on a fully diluted basis. The agreed transaction values reflect the parties’ mutual recognition of the strategic value of their respective businesses and are not based solely on prevailing market prices. The definitive agreements advance the transaction from the previously announced non-binding term sheet to a signed contractual framework. The special stock dividend mechanism contemplated in the earlier term sheet is not part of the definitive transaction. Its removal simplifies the transaction structure and is intended to support efficient execution and closing. The parties’ agreed valuation of approximately $60 million for FFR reflects its Nasdaq-listed platform, existing shareholder base and trading infrastructure, relatively simple balance sheet and capitalization structure, existing RoboShare business, and financial assets, including cash, cash equivalents, note receivables and certain investments, including investments in FFAI. FFR’s existing RoboShare platform also offers potential synergies with the acquired robotics business across sales, leasing, deployment and recurring services. Following the transaction, FFR will emerge as a Nasdaq-listed company with an established shareholder base, a relatively simple balance sheet, minimal debt, and no outstanding convertible notes, providing the robotics business with direct access to U.S. capital markets. Pryor Cashman serves as legal counsel to FFAI. Loeb & Loeb LLP serves as legal counsel to the FFR Special Committee. Advanture Capital Solutions LLC is acting as independent financial advisor to FFR’s Special Committee and has rendered a fairness opinion to FFR’s Special Committee. FFR Has Secured Up to $10 Million in PIPE Financing with No Discount FFR has secured up to $10 million in first-round PIPE financing. The financing is priced at market, with no discount, no warrants, and low associated financing costs, and is structured to minimize equity dilution. To best support investor interests, FFR limited the offering to approximately $10 million to meet its current funding needs while reducing unnecessary equity dilution. Upon closing, on an as-converted, fully diluted basis, FFAI will hold approximately 65.7% of FFR, with all newly issued shares received in this transaction subject to an 18-month lockup. Management and employees will hold approximately 18.2%, PIPE investors approximately 5.5%, and other FFR stockholders approximately 10.7%. PIPE investors may not sell their shares within six months or before the resale registration statement becomes effective. FFAI, management and employees, and PIPE investors will collectively hold approximately 89.3%. Excluding these holdings, the freely tradable public float will consist of approximately 13 million shares, representing approximately 10.7% of the total. These estimates are subject to confirmation and may change based on the final transaction capitalization and PIPE terms. The financing will further strengthen FFR’s capital base and provide resources to advance its “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” strategy, supporting product R&D, commercialization, and scaled deployment of the robotics ecosystem. Upon completion of the financing, the Company will have additional resources for business development, R&D investment, and market expansion. For stockholders and investors, lower financing costs and limited equity dilution are expected to further improve the Company’s capital structure and support the realization of the robotics business’s long-term value. FFR Aims to Achieve and Maintain a Top Three Comprehensive Ranking in the EAI Robotics Industry The Company is building a full-lifecycle robotics business spanning research and development, supply chain, manufacturing, sales, deployment, data, and operations, centered on its “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” ecosystem. Under preliminary projections prepared by FFAI management for the FF EAI Robotics business on a standalone basis, revenue is projected to reach approximately $7 million in 2026 and $45 million in 2027. The projections contemplate positive gross margin in 2026, gross margin of approximately 30% in 2027 and approximately 54% in 2030, cumulative revenue of approximately $1.98 billion from 2026 through 2030, and positive operating cash flow in the third quarter of 2028. Cumulative financing requirements before then are projected to be no more than $150 million, implying low dilution for stockholders and financing needs well below those of industry peers. FFAI management projects EAI Device sales of 2,001 units in 2026 and 7,400 units in 2027, with cumulative sales exceeding 130,000 units over five years. The projections also contemplate more than 19 million hours of cumulative data supply over five years and approximately $300 million in cumulative research and development investment over the same time period. As the EAI Brain and Developer Platform, Industry Productivity Solutions, EAI Data Factory and related services develop, ecosystem revenue is projected to grow from 22% of total revenue in 2026 to 49% by 2030. These projections were prepared by FFAI management and have not been adopted by FFR as Company guidance. Actual results may differ materially. Board, Governance Framework and Employee Incentives Support Leadership Continuity and Long-Term Execution To support the continuity and long-term execution of the robotics business after closing, the transaction includes arrangements covering employee incentives, key employee retention, governance, and Board composition. As part of these arrangements, outstanding employee stock-option incentives associated with the FF EAI Robotics business will be assumed and converted, at the agreed exchange ratio, into stock options of FFR. The structure is intended to align the long-term interests of the core team with FFR’s development and long-term value creation. Key employees are expected to be retained and to enter into employment agreements, which are important conditions to closing. Key management will continue to support both FFR and FFAI, helping preserve the talent and business capabilities needed to support the robotics business. Under preliminary projections prepared by FFAI management for the FF EAI Robotics business on a standalone basis, revenue is projected to reach approximately $7 million in 2026 and $45 million in 2027. The projections contemplate positive gross margin in 2026, gross margin of approximately 30% in 2027 and approximately 54% in 2030, cumulative revenue of approximately $1.98 billion from 2026 through 2030, and positive operating cash flow in the third quarter of 2028. Cumulative financing requirements before then are projected to be no more than $150 million, implying low dilution for stockholders and financing needs well below those of industry peers.

FFAI management projects EAI Device sales of 2,001 units in 2026 and 7,400 units in 2027, with cumulative sales exceeding 130,000 units over five years. The projections also contemplate more than 19 million hours of cumulative data supply over five years and approximately $300 million in cumulative research and development investment over the same time period.

As the EAI Brain and Developer Platform, Industry Productivity Solutions, EAI Data Factory and related services develop, ecosystem revenue is projected to grow from 22% of total revenue in 2026 to 49% by 2030. These projections were prepared by FFAI management and have not been adopted by FFR as Company guidance. Actual results may differ materially.
Board, Governance Framework and Employee Incentives Support Leadership Continuity and Long-Term Execution

To support the continuity and long-term execution of the robotics business after closing, the transaction includes arrangements covering employee incentives, key employee retention, governance, and Board composition. As part of these arrangements, outstanding employee stock-option incentives associated with the FF EAI Robotics business will be assumed and converted, at the agreed exchange ratio, into stock options of FFR. The structure is intended to align the long-term interests of the core team with FFR’s development and long-term value creation.

Key employees are expected to be retained and to enter into employment agreements, which are important conditions to closing. Key management will continue to support both FFR and FFAI, helping preserve the talent and business capabilities needed to support the robotics business.

FFR’s governance framework is expected to be similar to the governance arrangements between FF Global Partners LLC and FFAI, intended to support leadership continuity, strategic oversight and long-term execution under the founding team’s leadership, while providing additional protections at the Board level. The final arrangements will be described in FFR’s filings with the SEC.
Independent Listing Is Intended to Highlight the Value of the Robotics Business
For two years following closing, FFAI and its affiliates have agreed to observe non-competition restrictions in territories where FFR and its affiliates conduct robotics business.

For FFAI and its stockholders, the transaction anchors the agreed value of the robotics business and releases it through a standalone public-company platform, while FFAI is expected to be the majority and controlling stockholder of FFR and continues to participate in the robotics business.

Next, FFAI will work with FFR to advance the transaction closing in an orderly manner. The closing is expected to be completed by the end of October. Upon completion of the transaction, FFAI will announce its next-stage strategy and business plan.

“This agreement will help us grow the business, develop our technology, and build our AI systems,” said YT Jia, Founder and Global Chief Executive Officer of Faraday Future. “This marks a new beginning for both companies and an important step for EAI and Physical AI as they move from exploration to building an industry together, and making a major leap forward, which will give the robotics business a dedicated public-company platform alongside RoboShare’s capabilities.”

extraction.body: Faraday Future Announces That It Has Signed a Definitive Agreement with FFR to Combine FFAI’s Full Robotics Business at Approx. $200 Million Valuation and $2.246 Per Share, Representing Approximately 50 Percent Premium Faraday Future Announces that it has Signed a Definitive Agreement with FFR to Combine FFAI’s Full Robotics Business at Approx. $200 Million Valuation and $2.246 Per Share, Representing Approximately 50 Percent Premium. LOS ANGELES--( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc. (NASDAQ: FFAI) (“Faraday Future,” “FF,” or the “Company”), a California-based global Embodied AI (“EAI”) ecosystem company, today announced that it has signed definitive agreements with FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR) (renamed from AIxCrypto Holdings, Inc. and AIXC) for FFR to acquire FFAI’s full robotics ecosystem business at an agreed valuation of approximately $200 million. The transaction advances the parties’ previously announced transaction process to the definitive agreement stage. Its structure has been simplified to facilitate execution and closing. Following closing, FFR will become the first U.S.-listed pure-play “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” humanoid and bionic EAI robotics ecosystem company, with the goal of maintaining a top three overall ranking in the EAI robotics industry over the next five years. FFAI plans to adopt an upgraded operating model inspired by Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet and upgrade from EAI vehicle manufacturing to a Robotaxi Sharing Network and AI VisiCabin technology operator, joining forces with RoboShare to build a lighter-asset shared mobility model. Following the strategic upgrade, FFAI plans to work with RoboShare to expand shared mobility, Robotaxi and EAI cabin businesses; explore integrating FF’s “3rd aiSpace” (Intelligent Cabin) into shared vehicles; and facilitate the connection of FFAI vehicles to the Robotaxi network. These efforts are intended to create synergies among vehicles, cabin experiences, and shared operations. By leveraging RoboShare’s sharing platform and operational capabilities, FFAI also plans to pursue opportunities in vehicle-asset onboarding, operations and user services. Share Issuance at $2.246 per Share, a Premium to FFR’s Market Price Under the definitive agreements, the parties agreed on a valuation of approximately $200 million for FFAI’s robotics business and approximately $60 million for FFR on a fully diluted basis. The agreed transaction values reflect the parties’ mutual recognition of the strategic value of their respective businesses and are not based solely on prevailing market prices. The definitive agreements advance the transaction from the previously announced non-binding term sheet to a signed contractual framework. The special stock dividend mechanism contemplated in the earlier term sheet is not part of the definitive transaction. Its removal simplifies the transaction structure and is intended to support efficient execution and closing. The parties’ agreed valuation of approximately $60 million for FFR reflects its Nasdaq-listed platform, existing shareholder base and trading infrastructure, relatively simple balance sheet and capitalization structure, existing RoboShare business, and financial assets, including cash, cash equivalents, note receivables and certain investments, including investments in FFAI. FFR’s existing RoboShare platform also offers potential synergies with the acquired robotics business across sales, leasing, deployment and recurring services. Following the transaction, FFR will emerge as a Nasdaq-listed company with an established shareholder base, a relatively simple balance sheet, minimal debt, and no outstanding convertible notes, providing the robotics business with direct access to U.S. capital markets. Pryor Cashman serves as legal counsel to FFAI. Loeb & Loeb LLP serves as legal counsel to the FFR Special Committee. Advanture Capital Solutions LLC is acting as independent financial advisor to FFR’s Special Committee and has rendered a fairness opinion to FFR’s Special Committee. FFR Has Secured Up to $10 Million in PIPE Financing with No Discount FFR has secured up to $10 million in first-round PIPE financing. The financing is priced at market, with no discount, no warrants, and low associated financing costs, and is structured to minimize equity dilution. To best support investor interests, FFR limited the offering to approximately $10 million to meet its current funding needs while reducing unnecessary equity dilution. Upon closing, on an as-converted, fully diluted basis, FFAI will hold approximately 65.7% of FFR, with all newly issued shares received in this transaction subject to an 18-month lockup. Management and employees will hold approximately 18.2%, PIPE investors approximately 5.5%, and other FFR stockholders approximately 10.7%. PIPE investors may not sell their shares within six months or before the resale registration statement becomes effective. FFAI, management and employees, and PIPE investors will collectively hold approximately 89.3%. Excluding these holdings, the freely tradable public float will consist of approximately 13 million shares, representing approximately 10.7% of the total. These estimates are subject to confirmation and may change based on the final transaction capitalization and PIPE terms. The financing will further strengthen FFR’s capital base and provide resources to advance its “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” strategy, supporting product R&D, commercialization, and scaled deployment of the robotics ecosystem. Faraday Future Announces that it has Signed a Definitive Agreement with FFR to Combine FFAI’s Full Robotics Business at Approx. $200 Million Valuation and $2.246 Per Share, Representing Approximately 50 Percent Premium.

LOS ANGELES--( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc. (NASDAQ: FFAI) (“Faraday Future,” “FF,” or the “Company”), a California-based global Embodied AI (“EAI”) ecosystem company, today announced that it has signed definitive agreements with FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR) (renamed from AIxCrypto Holdings, Inc. and AIXC) for FFR to acquire FFAI’s full robotics ecosystem business at an agreed valuation of approximately $200 million.

The transaction advances the parties’ previously announced transaction process to the definitive agreement stage. Its structure has been simplified to facilitate execution and closing. Following closing, FFR will become the first U.S.-listed pure-play “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” humanoid and bionic EAI robotics ecosystem company, with the goal of maintaining a top three overall ranking in the EAI robotics industry over the next five years.

FFAI plans to adopt an upgraded operating model inspired by Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet and upgrade from EAI vehicle manufacturing to a Robotaxi Sharing Network and AI VisiCabin technology operator, joining forces with RoboShare to build a lighter-asset shared mobility model. Following the strategic upgrade, FFAI plans to work with RoboShare to expand shared mobility, Robotaxi and EAI cabin businesses; explore integrating FF’s “3rd aiSpace” (Intelligent Cabin) into shared vehicles; and facilitate the connection of FFAI vehicles to the Robotaxi network. These efforts are intended to create synergies among vehicles, cabin experiences, and shared operations. By leveraging RoboShare’s sharing platform and operational capabilities, FFAI also plans to pursue opportunities in vehicle-asset onboarding, operations and user services.
Share Issuance at $2.246 per Share, a Premium to FFR’s Market Price

Under the definitive agreements, the parties agreed on a valuation of approximately $200 million for FFAI’s robotics business and approximately $60 million for FFR on a fully diluted basis. The agreed transaction values reflect the parties’ mutual recognition of the strategic value of their respective businesses and are not based solely on prevailing market prices.

The definitive agreements advance the transaction from the previously announced non-binding term sheet to a signed contractual framework. The special stock dividend mechanism contemplated in the earlier term sheet is not part of the definitive transaction. Its removal simplifies the transaction structure and is intended to support efficient execution and closing.

The parties’ agreed valuation of approximately $60 million for FFR reflects its Nasdaq-listed platform, existing shareholder base and trading infrastructure, relatively simple balance sheet and capitalization structure, existing RoboShare business, and financial assets, including cash, cash equivalents, note receivables and certain investments, including investments in FFAI. FFR’s existing RoboShare platform also offers potential synergies with the acquired robotics business across sales, leasing, deployment and recurring services. Following the transaction, FFR will emerge as a Nasdaq-listed company with an established shareholder base, a relatively simple balance sheet, minimal debt, and no outstanding convertible notes, providing the robotics business with direct access to U.S. capital markets.

Pryor Cashman serves as legal counsel to FFAI. Loeb & Loeb LLP serves as legal counsel to the FFR Special Committee. Advanture Capital Solutions LLC is acting as independent financial advisor to FFR’s Special Committee and has rendered a fairness opinion to FFR’s Special Committee.
FFR Has Secured Up to $10 Million in PIPE Financing with No Discount

FFR has secured up to $10 million in first-round PIPE financing. The financing is priced at market, with no discount, no warrants, and low associated financing costs, and is structured to minimize equity dilution. To best support investor interests, FFR limited the offering to approximately $10 million to meet its current funding needs while reducing unnecessary equity dilution.

Upon closing, on an as-converted, fully diluted basis, FFAI will hold approximately 65.7% of FFR, with all newly issued shares received in this transaction subject to an 18-month lockup. Management and employees will hold approximately 18.2%, PIPE investors approximately 5.5%, and other FFR stockholders approximately 10.7%. PIPE investors may not sell their shares within six months or before the resale registration statement becomes effective. FFAI, management and employees, and PIPE investors will collectively hold approximately 89.3%. Excluding these holdings, the freely tradable public float will consist of approximately 13 million shares, representing approximately 10.7% of the total.
These estimates are subject to confirmation and may change based on the final transaction capitalization and PIPE terms.

The financing will further strengthen FFR’s capital base and provide resources to advance its “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” strategy, supporting product R&D, commercialization, and scaled deployment of the robotics ecosystem.

Upon completion of the financing, the Company will have additional resources for business development, R&D investment, and market expansion. For stockholders and investors, lower financing costs and limited equity dilution are expected to further improve the Company’s capital structure and support the realization of the robotics business’s long-term value.
FFR Aims to Achieve and Maintain a Top Three Comprehensive Ranking in the EAI Robotics Industry

The Company is building a full-lifecycle robotics business spanning research and development, supply chain, manufacturing, sales, deployment, data, and operations, centered on its “Four-Core Full-Stack AI” ecosystem.

Under preliminary projections prepared by FFAI management for the FF EAI Robotics business on a standalone basis, revenue is projected to reach approximately $7 million in 2026 and $45 million in 2027. The projections contemplate positive gross margin in 2026, gross margin of approximately 30% in 2027 and approximately 54% in 2030, cumulative revenue of approximately $1.98 billion from 2026 through 2030, and positive operating cash flow in the third quarter of 2028. Cumulative financing requirements before then are projected to be no more than $150 million, implying low dilution for stockholders and financing needs well below those of industry peers.

FFAI management projects EAI Device sales of 2,001 units in 2026 and 7,400 units in 2027, with cumulative sales exceeding 130,000 units over five years. The projections also contemplate more than 19 million hours of cumulative data supply over five years and approximately $300 million in cumulative research and development investment over the same time period.

As the EAI Brain and Developer Platform, Industry Productivity Solutions, EAI Data Factory and related services develop, ecosystem revenue is projected to grow from 22% of total revenue in 2026 to 49% by 2030. These projections were prepared by FFAI management and have not been adopted by FFR as Company guidance. Actual results may differ materially.
Board, Governance Framework and Employee Incentives Support Leadership Continuity and Long-Term Execution

To support the continuity and long-term execution of the robotics business after closing, the transaction includes arrangements covering employee incentives, key employee retention, governance, and Board composition. As part of these arrangements, outstanding employee stock-option incentives associated with the FF EAI Robotics business will be assumed and converted, at the agreed exchange ratio, into stock options of FFR. The structure is intended to align the long-term interests of the core team with FFR’s development and long-term value creation.

Key employees are expected to be retained and to enter into employment agreements, which are important conditions to closing. Key management will continue to support both FFR and FFAI, helping preserve the talent and business capabilities needed to support the robotics business.

FFR’s governance framework is expected to be similar to the governance arrangements between FF Global Partners LLC and FFAI, intended to support leadership continuity, strategic oversight and long-term execution under the founding team’s leadership, while providing additional protections at the Board level. The final arrangements will be described in FFR’s filings with the SEC.
Independent Listing Is Intended to Highlight the Value of the Robotics Business
For two years following closing, FFAI and its affiliates have agreed to observe non-competition restrictions in territories where FFR and its affiliates conduct robotics business.

For FFAI and its stockholders, the transaction anchors the agreed value of the robotics business and releases it through a standalone public-company platform, while FFAI is expected to be the majority and controlling stockholder of FFR and continues to participate in the robotics business.

Next, FFAI will work with FFR to advance the transaction closing in an orderly manner. The closing is expected to be completed by the end of October. Upon completion of the transaction, FFAI will announce its next-stage strategy and business plan.

“This agreement will help us grow the business, develop our technology, and build our AI systems,” said YT Jia, Founder and Global Chief Executive Officer of Faraday Future. “This marks a new beginning for both companies and an important step for EAI and Physical AI as they move from exploration to building an industry together, and making a major leap forward, which will give the robotics business a dedicated public-company platform alongside RoboShare’s capabilities.”

First, for FF stockholders, the plan is intended to maximize long-term stockholder value. By linking the core team’s incentives to the growth of the robotics business, FF aims to strengthen operating efficiency and value creation while keeping stockholder interests at the forefront.

Second, for the Company, the plan is expected to strengthen its ability to attract and retain top talent, encourage an entrepreneurial and partnership-oriented culture, and build the team needed to compete in the robotics industry.

Finally, for the industry, FF EAI Robotics aims to become the first robotics company to implement a partnership model, offering an example of how long-term talent incentives can strengthen organizational capabilities across the robotics sector.

sources.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
passages: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown.
Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models.
Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware.

Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.

This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads?
Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target.
Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it.
Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators.
The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells.
The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts.
A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job.

Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps.
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop.
In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days).
Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”
Such transparency is particularly important to avoid conflating the demonstrated capability to replicate with an emerging threat of autonomous self-replication.”
“Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.”
“These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said.

It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs.
For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed.

extraction.body: “Small weight-based replicators” could usher in a new generation of computer worms. AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output. The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against. This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it. “Such an ‘AI worm’ could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware,” Anthropic said . “Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.” Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators. The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells. The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts. A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job. Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps. Anthropic said the dynamic inference setup is the least studied and likely most challenging stage in the replication cycle. It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs. “These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said. The experiment shows that small models are becoming increasingly capable at solving those problems autonomously. At the moment, however, none of the light-weight models tested are able to mount end-to-end replication, meaning discovering new devices, using an exploit to gain access to them, infecting them with a payload, configuring an inference server, and repeating the process. The process is also painfully slow; Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over the 15 Android TV boxes, performed at just 0.39 tokens per second. That translates to a full-inference setup time of 71 to 150 hours for an unoptimized Gemma4-26B-A4B and 29 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B. (The researchers said that the large model GLM-5.2 appears to be able to do so reliably.) The company said that 30B-parameter models can already complete many of the individual replication steps now, although they make mistakes when performing end-to-end replication. The company went on to say that if small models continue to improve at their current pace, they may be able to achieve the same limited results by the end of the year and that “small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.” The experiment leaves a variety of important considerations unanswered. For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed. This tool is used during development and debugging but should never be used in production settings, because it gives attackers access to the entire device stack. And for another, the replication wasn’t performed by the small models themselves, but rather with GLM-5.2 to orchestrate the process while the targets ran a smaller Llama model. Ultimately, the experiment demonstrates that small agentic models are becoming capable of setting up complex, distributed inference infrastructures across multiple machines. What remains to be established, however, is whether these models would initiate self-replication on their own. “Despite the well-designed experimental setup, the study does not, on its own, establish that small models would autonomously choose to replicate,” AI researcher Xiaohan Fu said in an interview. “Providing reproducible agent setups, including the exact prompts and instructions given to the models, would help the research community better understand the findings and assess their implications. AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown.

By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.

Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”

Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.

The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against.

This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it.

“Such an ‘AI worm’ could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware,” Anthropic said . “Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.”

Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators. The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells. The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts. A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job. Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps.

Anthropic said the dynamic inference setup is the least studied and likely most challenging stage in the replication cycle. It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs.
“These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said.

The experiment shows that small models are becoming increasingly capable at solving those problems autonomously. At the moment, however, none of the light-weight models tested are able to mount end-to-end replication, meaning discovering new devices, using an exploit to gain access to them, infecting them with a payload, configuring an inference server, and repeating the process. The process is also painfully slow; Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over the 15 Android TV boxes, performed at just 0.39 tokens per second. That translates to a full-inference setup time of 71 to 150 hours for an unoptimized Gemma4-26B-A4B and 29 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B. (The researchers said that the large model GLM-5.2 appears to be able to do so reliably.)

The company said that 30B-parameter models can already complete many of the individual replication steps now, although they make mistakes when performing end-to-end replication. The company went on to say that if small models continue to improve at their current pace, they may be able to achieve the same limited results by the end of the year and that “small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.”

The experiment leaves a variety of important considerations unanswered. For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed. This tool is used during development and debugging but should never be used in production settings, because it gives attackers access to the entire device stack. And for another, the replication wasn’t performed by the small models themselves, but rather with GLM-5.2 to orchestrate the process while the targets ran a smaller Llama model.

Ultimately, the experiment demonstrates that small agentic models are becoming capable of setting up complex, distributed inference infrastructures across multiple machines. What remains to be established, however, is whether these models would initiate self-replication on their own.

“Despite the well-designed experimental setup, the study does not, on its own, establish that small models would autonomously choose to replicate,” AI researcher Xiaohan Fu said in an interview. “Providing reproducible agent setups, including the exact prompts and instructions given to the models, would help the research community better understand the findings and assess their implications. Such transparency is particularly important to avoid conflating the demonstrated capability to replicate with an emerging threat of autonomous self-replication.”

sources.title: Anthropic warns small AI models may soon self-replicate across connected devices - The News International
passages: Anthropic warns small AI models could soon autonomously self-replicating across poorly secured smart devices, raising major containment and security concerns
It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication.
Anthropic has urged developers and manufacturers to significantly harden baseline security across consumer electronics to mitigate future loss-of-control risks.

Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data center processors, Anthropic warned.
Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources.
In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication.

The leading American AI safety and research company setup also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after.
The firm focused on IoT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances, and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured.

coreStoryFacts.text: Experiments show cheap TV boxes can run capable AI models, and small models may soon be able to spread across such devices on their own.
Copyright © 2026 SecurityWeek ®, a Wired Business Media Publication.

AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown.
Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models.
Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware.

Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.

This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads?
Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target.
Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it.
Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators.
The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells.
The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts.
A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job.

Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps.
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop.
In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days).
Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”
Such transparency is particularly important to avoid conflating the demonstrated capability to replicate with an emerging threat of autonomous self-replication.”
“Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.”
“These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said.

It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs.
For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed.

AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output. The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4GB of memory, to achieve inference. The Qwen3.5-9B was able to configure other LLMs to run on eight of nine hardware types. Unlike traditional malware, which must be written to run on specific hardware or software, the model was able to use its weights to make configurations on the fly that were specific to the devices it was tested against. This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it. “Such an ‘AI worm’ could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware,” Anthropic said . “Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.” Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators. The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells. The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts. A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job. Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps. Anthropic said the dynamic inference setup is the least studied and likely most challenging stage in the replication cycle. It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs. “These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said. The experiment shows that small models are becoming increasingly capable at solving those problems autonomously. At the moment, however, none of the light-weight models tested are able to mount end-to-end replication, meaning discovering new devices, using an exploit to gain access to them, infecting them with a payload, configuring an inference server, and repeating the process. The process is also painfully slow; Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over the 15 Android TV boxes, performed at just 0.39 tokens per second. That translates to a full-inference setup time of 71 to 150 hours for an unoptimized Gemma4-26B-A4B and 29 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B. (The researchers said that the large model GLM-5.2 appears to be able to do so reliably.) The company said that 30B-parameter models can already complete many of the individual replication steps now, although they make mistakes when performing end-to-end replication. The company went on to say that if small models continue to improve at their current pace, they may be able to achieve the same limited results by the end of the year and that “small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.” The experiment leaves a variety of important considerations unanswered. For one, the Android devices targeted by small models had an unauthenticated Android Debug Bridge exposed. This tool is used during development and debugging but should never be used in production settings, because it gives attackers access to the entire device stack. And for another, the replication wasn’t performed by the small models themselves, but rather with GLM-5.2 to orchestrate the process while the targets ran a smaller Llama model. Ultimately, the experiment demonstrates that small agentic models are becoming capable of setting up complex, distributed inference infrastructures across multiple machines. What remains to be established, however, is whether these models would initiate self-replication on their own. “Despite the well-designed experimental setup, the study does not, on its own, establish that small models would autonomously choose to replicate,” AI researcher Xiaohan Fu said in an interview. “Providing reproducible agent setups, including the exact prompts and instructions given to the models, would help the research community better understand the findings and assess their implications. Ultimately, the experiment demonstrates that small agentic models are becoming capable of setting up complex, distributed inference infrastructures across multiple machines. What remains to be established, however, is whether these models would initiate self-replication on their own.

“Despite the well-designed experimental setup, the study does not, on its own, establish that small models would autonomously choose to replicate,” AI researcher Xiaohan Fu said in an interview. “Providing reproducible agent setups, including the exact prompts and instructions given to the models, would help the research community better understand the findings and assess their implications. Such transparency is particularly important to avoid conflating the demonstrated capability to replicate with an emerging threat of autonomous self-replication.”

Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models.
Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware.

Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.

This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai , install DDoS code and other payloads?
Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target.
Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it.
Anthropic called these autonomous worms small weight-based replicators.
The models ran agents that had access to common exploitation tools, like reverse shells.
The flow of the attacks was (1) finding targets, (2) gaining code execution, (3) establishing inference, and (4) propagating to new hosts.
A key benefit over traditional worms is what Anthropic said is the agents’ ability to learn on the job.

Each time an AI replicator fails to compromise a specific platform device, it can leave a list of prompts, code, and notes to future replicators so they don’t waste time reusing the same ineffective steps.
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop.

Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”

“Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.”
“These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from,” Anthropic said.

It requires a long sequence of decisions based on the specific hardware and software of each target and involves selecting compatible inference software, installing dependencies, and debugging platform-specific bugs.

passages: ▲ Artificial Intelligence (AI) Anthropic has warned that even small artificial intelligence (AI) models could reach a level as early as the end of this year where they operate like "computer viruses," copying themselves and spreading across household appliances.

In a research report released on October 12 (local time), Anthropic stated, "It may be only a few months before small AI models acquire the capability to self-replicate across Internet of Things (IoT) devices, such as smart ovens or low-cost Android TV boxes." Anthropic explained that because such self-replicating AI spreads and operates scattered across numerous devices, it is difficult to stop because there is no central shutdown point—unlike general AI services where turning off a few servers is enough.
Even a small AI model with 9 billion parameters succeeded on 8 out of 9 tested devices.

According to Reuters, Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), evaluated the Anthropic report, saying, "Succeeding in running a small model on a cheap TV does not constitute a security crisis," and calling it "an interesting technical paper mixed with no small amount of vendor hype." Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), said, "We don't know yet how likely it is that such a thing will actually happen," adding, "It is not zero, but it is not certain either." (Photo: Yonhap News, Getty Images) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.
On the same day, an Anthropic co-founder advanced the projected timeline by a year, stating that AI reaching the stage of self-improvement could become possible next year.

Calling this an "AI worm," Anthropic conducted a three-stage verification experiment. 75,000 KRW) each, connected them, and installed Google's AI model "Gemma 4" across them. Second, they tested whether the AI could independently install and operate another AI model on an unfamiliar device. Even a small AI model with 9 billion parameters succeeded on 8 out of 9 tested devices. Finally, they created a test network using 8 virtual devices and had the AI planted in the first device autonomously repeat the process of locating, installing, and operating AI on the other devices. In 5 rounds of testing, only Zhipu AI's "GLM-5.2" from China succeeded in migrating to all 8 devices in 4 rounds, and up to 7 devices in 1 round. While acknowledging that a fully self-replicating AI does not yet exist and that the speed of replication spread would be slow, Anthropic projected that under current development trends, small models could reach the level of GLM-5.2 by the end of this year and become capable of direct self-replication inside devices. Anthropic explained that a realistic worst-case scenario is a "swarm" form where multiple types of AI mix various devices and replication methods. Going beyond the scope of the experiments, the company stated it anticipates "a future where agents run on all kinds of hardware, including things outside of human control." Jack Clark, co-founder and head of policy at Anthropic, stated in a newsletter titled "Import AI" published the same day, "It is more likely that full recursive self-improvement (RSI) will become possible next year," adding, "Previously, I thought 2028 was more likely." Clark based his assessment on test results from the AI safety research organization P-Zero Research, noting that for AI to improve itself, a researcher's "intuition" in choosing which experiments to run and interpreting the results is key, and this capability is improving rapidly. In these tests, AI models designed experiments and interpreted results for actual AI development tasks such as training data selection and language model training. This capability has doubled approximately every three months since December of last year. sources.title: Anthropic warns small AI models may soon self-replicate across connected devices - The News International
passages: Anthropic warns small AI models could soon autonomously self-replicating across poorly secured smart devices, raising major containment and security concerns
It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication.
Anthropic has urged developers and manufacturers to significantly harden baseline security across consumer electronics to mitigate future loss-of-control risks.

Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data center processors, Anthropic warned.
Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources.
In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication.

The leading American AI safety and research company setup also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after.
The firm focused on IoT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances, and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured.

The Social Security Administration will announce the official annual cost-of-living-adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday, Oct. 14, following the Bureau of Labor Statistics' release of September inflation data. Recipients will receive their personalized notices detailing their new benefit amounts in December. According to a forecast from The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), the adjustment is projected to be 3.5% in 2027, down 0.1 percentage point from last month's forecast of 3.6%. This forecast is also in line with projections from Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst. Johnson told CNBC that the Social Security COLA for 2027 could be 3.5%, though the final figure could change due to volatile oil prices. "The biggest thing we're watching with the COLA announcement coming are short-term shocks to the economy that push inflation way up or down in the next 30 days," TSCL executive director Shannon Benton said in a statement. "Of the three CPI-W figures used to calculate the COLA, two are already in." If TSCL's projections are correct, a 3.5% COLA would boost the average retiree's monthly check by $67.90, from $1,940.08 to $2,007.98. COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). The point of these adjustments is to ensure that Social Security benefits keep up with inflation. This forecast comes after the release of August's Consumer Price Index (CPI), which showed a 3.4% year-over-year increase in consumer prices. Gas prices spiked 3.9% last month amid the ongoing war between the U.S. and Iran, and "core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% month over month. If TSCL's projection holds, it would mark the largest COLA increase in four years. Still — experts say it could be a letdown for seniors. "No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run," said Benton. "The reality is that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently. The CPI-W captures the experience of urban wage earners, which doesn't represent the average senior's budget." A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective. If there is an increase, it must be rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent. If there is no increase, or if the rounded increase is zero, there is no COLA for the year. You can find out exactly how much your benefits will increase by creating an account on SSA.gov . After verifying your account, you'll be able to get an estimate of your retirement benefits and see how those benefits may change depending on your retirement age. You can also crunch the numbers yourself and calculate your new Social Security benefit by multiplying the percentage increase by your current monthly benefit amount. Say you're receiving $2,071, which is around the current average monthly benefit for retirees according to the SSA. When multiplied by the estimated COLA of 3.5% or 0.035%, you can expect a monthly benefit of about $2,143.48 — about a $72 increase. extraction.body: The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment will be 3.6% in 2027, the Social Security Administration said on Wednesday. The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, provides an annual inflation adjustment to both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, benefits. Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average, the agency said. "Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement. Around 72 million Social Security recipients will see the benefit increases in January, according to SSA. About 7.3 million SSI beneficiaries will receive higher payments starting Dec. 31, the agency said. The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is in line with Social Security experts' projections , which last month forecast an increase of 3.5% to 3.6%. The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. That year, beneficiaries received an 8.7% benefit boost — the highest in four decades — in response to rising inflation. New government inflation data released on Wednesday shows consumer price increases are accelerating. The consumer price index rose 3.7% over the past 12 months, as gas prices jumped. About 40% of Social Security beneficiaries ages 65 and over rely on the program for at least half of their income, according to the AARP . A recent AARP survey found 76% of respondents said a 3.5% COLA would not be enough . The Social Security COLA is "critically important" because it helps millions of Americans cover rising everyday costs, including groceries, routine bills and health care, AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement. "There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," Minter-Jordan said. Beneficiaries can multiply their current monthly benefit amount by 3.6%, or 0.036, to estimate the increase to their checks for 2027. However, keep in mind that increases to Medicare Part B or Part D premiums for 2027 — which may be deducted directly from benefit checks — can affect the size of beneficiaries' monthly payments. Standard monthly premiums for Medicare Part B are projected to be $209.50 in 2027 , up from $202.90 in 2026, according to a report from Medicare trustees. Some beneficiaries may pay extra surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, or IRMAAs, if they have higher incomes. Medicare Part B covers medically necessary and preventive services. Meanwhile, Medicare Part D prescription drug plans may see modest premium increases in 2027, according to an analysis by KFF , a nonpartisan health policy research group. The Social Security Administration will send beneficiaries notices about the COLA changes. The notices will include specific information about their 2027 benefits, including exact payment dates and dollar amounts, as well as any deductions. Individuals who have created online My Social Security accounts can access that information starting in late November, according to the agency. Beneficiaries without an online account who want to see their COLA notice online must create an account and opt into paperless notices by Nov. 18. Beneficiaries who have not signed up to receive online notices will receive mailed COLA statements in December. Those individuals should make sure the address the agency has on file is up to date, according to SSA. Medicare premium amounts for 2027 will also be available online through the My Social Security message center starting in late November, the agency said. The COLA is based on the percentage increase of one specific government inflation measure — the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W — from the third quarter of the previous year to the third quarter of the current year. The CPI-W is a subset of the consumer price index that tracks the average change in prices for goods and services purchased by urban households. The CPI-W rose 3.9% over the past 12 months, according to September data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Wednesday. Policymakers and advocates have proposed alternatives to the CPI-W for calculating the annual COLA. One alternative is the chained CPI, an index that accounts for changes in buying habits as prices rise. However, a recent AARP analysis found that switching to that measure would "substantially lower benefits over time." Others have proposed using the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E, an experimental index that tracks spending for individuals ages 62 and over. However, some experts say the CPI-E does not necessarily grow much faster than the current measure used to calculate benefit increases. Switching to a different COLA measure is among the changes lawmakers may consider in upcoming Social Security reform. "Social Security's future is on the ballot this November, and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments," said Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group focused on expanding Social Security. extraction.body: Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure . The Social Security Administration will announce the official annual cost-of-living-adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday, Oct. 14, following the Bureau of Labor Statistics' release of September inflation data. Recipients will receive their personalized notices detailing their new benefit amounts in December. According to a forecast from The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), the adjustment is projected to be 3.5% in 2027, down 0.1 percentage point from last month's forecast of 3.6%. This forecast is also in line with projections from Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst. Johnson told CNBC that the Social Security COLA for 2027 could be 3.5%, though the final figure could change due to volatile oil prices. "The biggest thing we're watching with the COLA announcement coming are short-term shocks to the economy that push inflation way up or down in the next 30 days," TSCL executive director Shannon Benton said in a statement. "Of the three CPI-W figures used to calculate the COLA, two are already in." If TSCL's projections are correct, a 3.5% COLA would boost the average retiree's monthly check by $67.90, from $1,940.08 to $2,007.98. COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). The point of these adjustments is to ensure that Social Security benefits keep up with inflation. This forecast comes after the release of August's Consumer Price Index (CPI), which showed a 3.4% year-over-year increase in consumer prices. Gas prices spiked 3.9% last month amid the ongoing war between the U.S. and Iran, and "core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% month over month. If TSCL's projection holds, it would mark the largest COLA increase in four years. Still — experts say it could be a letdown for seniors. "No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run," said Benton. "The reality is that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently. The CPI-W captures the experience of urban wage earners, which doesn't represent the average senior's budget." A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective. If there is an increase, it must be rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent. If there is no increase, or if the rounded increase is zero, there is no COLA for the year. You can find out exactly how much your benefits will increase by creating an account on SSA.gov . After verifying your account, you'll be able to get an estimate of your retirement benefits and see how those benefits may change depending on your retirement age. You can also crunch the numbers yourself and calculate your new Social Security benefit by multiplying the percentage increase by your current monthly benefit amount. Say you're receiving $2,071, which is around the current average monthly benefit for retirees according to the SSA. When multiplied by the estimated COLA of 3.5% or 0.035%, you can expect a monthly benefit of about $2,143.48 — about a $72 increase.
