There’s quite a few reasons for the market plunge. Strategy broke a years-long rule and sold Bitcoin for the first time in nearly four years, while U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs are now on their longest outflow streak ever. On top of that, $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, and fresh U.S. strikes on Iran have rattled the fragile ceasefire that had been holding since April. Every major coin is now down double digits on the month. Below is the breakdown of how Bitcoin, Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) are performing right now. Bitcoin is showing the worst of the market downturn. The largest cryptocurrency by market cap is now trading at $63,436, down 3.2% in 24 hours and down 22.3% on the month. The bigger picture is even worse, with Bitcoin trading more than 50% below its $126,000 all-time high. Meanwhile, Ethereum and XRP are doing no better. ETH is trading at $1,768 after a 25.8% slide on the month, and XRP at $1.17 has hit a 15-week low, down 17.3% on the month. Both followed Bitcoin’s slide and ended up losing even more ground. Solana took the hardest single-day hit of the four cryptocurrencies. SOL is down 4.6% in 24 hours alone and 20.9% over the past month, now trading at $68.38. High-beta altcoins like Solana and XRP amplify Bitcoin’s moves, and on the way down, that means they fall steeper than the rest of the market. Beyond the price drops, the leverage washout was also ugly. $1.76 billion in leveraged positions got liquidated in 24 hours, with $1.50 billion of that from long positions getting forced out. Bitcoin took $773 million of the damage, Ethereum $482 million, and Solana $88 million. Traders went into this week heavily long, and the market punished them for it. For nearly four years, Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy) was the loudest voice in Bitcoin, telling everyone to buy and never sell. The company built its corporate identity around accumulation, stacking 843,706 BTC over five years and turning Michael Saylor into the face of the institutional bullish thesis on Bitcoin. On Monday, that changed. Strategy disclosed in an SEC 8-K filing on June 1 that it had sold 32 Bitcoin between May 26 and May 31 for $2.5 million, at an average price of $77,135. The amount represents 0.004% of the company’s holdings. That is not a number that moves markets on its own, but the signal it sent did. That said, this was actually not panic selling. Saylor pre-announced the move on May 5, telling investors that Strategy would probably sell some bitcoin to pay a dividend just to inoculate the market and send the message that “we did it.” The 32 BTC went to fund distributions on STRC, which is the company’s perpetual preferred stock. So, the whole sequence was planned and telegraphed for weeks. However, none of that planning protected the stock. MSTR fell nearly 6% on Monday, then dropped another 7% on Wednesday as Bitcoin slid below $62,000. Two Wall Street analysts called the sale economically immaterial, but the narrative break was the bigger damage. For years, the “Saylor never sells” rule had been one of the arguments for holding Bitcoin through volatility. But the recent sale has made that argument look weaker, and the timing came right in the middle of the Bitcoin ETF outflow streak and a macro shock. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs were already on a record streak when last week ended, and they have now extended it further. The 10-day outflow run that closed May has stretched to 13 trading days as of June 3, deepening what was already the longest withdrawal streak since the funds launched in January 2024. The structural bid that had supported Bitcoin through every previous selloff is now selling instead of buying. The pace has been intense. On June 3 alone, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $396.6 million, led by BlackRock’s IBIT at $342.3 million and Fidelity’s FBTC at $54.3 million. And the day before, outflows hit $519 million. Since May 20, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost over $3 billion in cumulative net outflows, or roughly 40,000 BTC by holdings. Bitcoin ETF assets under management have dropped from around $109 billion to $85 billion during the streak, marking a 22% decline in three weeks. Ethereum ETFs have run their own parallel bleed, posting their 17th consecutive outflow day on June 3, with cumulative net inflows shrinking to $11.24 billion. The selling is not only happening in ETFs either. According to on-chain data, whales holding between 10 and 10,000 Bitcoin sold roughly 25,000 BTC in the past week alone. So it’s not just an ETF problem, but a wider sell-off happening across the board. Macro conditions have only made things worse for crypto. Inflation came in at 3.8% year-over-year in April, the hottest reading since May 2023, while wholesale prices jumped 6%, the largest increase since December 2022. Energy prices are up 17.9% on the year and gasoline is up 28.4%, which has pushed real wages negative for the first time since 2023. The Federal Reserve’s response has been to hold. The April FOMC vote was 8-4 to keep rates at 3.50%-3.75%, marking the most dissents since 1992. Markets are now pricing a 68.8% probability of zero rate cuts in all of 2026, according to Polymarket . New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, sworn in on May 22, has not had time to establish his own approach yet, which adds even more uncertainty. Then on Tuesday, June 2, Iran fired missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain, and the U.S. retaliated late that night with strikes on an Iranian military facility on Qeshm Island. Iranian drones hit Kuwait International Airport on Wednesday, killing one and injuring 63. Three days later, neither side has clarified whether the ceasefire still holds. The result keeps the inflation loop intact. WTI crude is at $94.99, and Brent at $97.07. The U.S. has drained 14% of its Strategic Petroleum Reserve trying to ease supply pressure. As long as oil stays at these levels, the Fed cannot cut, and as long as the Fed cannot cut, macro pressure will keep weighing on the crypto market. The selloff looks closer to capitulation than the start of a new leg down. Bitcoin tested $61,500 overnight and bounced, and that level is close to the 200-week moving average, which has held as support in past bear cycles. A 13-day ETF outflow streak, $1.76 billion in liquidations in a single day, and a narrative-breaking Strategy sale are the bearish drivers weighing on the market right now. But whether they mark a bottom or signal more downside is still unclear. Despite all that, there are a couple of events coming up this month that could change the bearish sentiment in the market. The next CPI release on June 10 will show whether inflation is cooling or staying sticky. Then the FOMC meeting on June 16-17 gives the first read on how Warsh sets policy and the updated dot plot. passages: Arbitrum's impressive 30-day gain is coupled with a severe drawdown and the smallest market cap at $1.27 billion.
Ethereum is worth about 240 times as much as Arbitrum, making ARB sensitive to trading volumes that wouldn't significantly affect larger assets like Ethereum or Bitcoin.
Consequently, ARB's price can rise rapidly when buyers enter the market and drop just as quickly when they pull back.
Arbitrum (CRYPTO:ARB) has gained 37.9%, rising to $0.19.
In contrast, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) rose 7.1% to $83,290, while Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH)—the blockchain Arbitrum is built on—fell 0.8% to $2,499.
With one coin performing well, another showing steady growth, and one struggling, which of Arbitrum, Bitcoin, or Ethereum is the better investment for the coming year?
Ethereum, with a market value of $305.12 billion, is down 49.5% from its all-time high.
It has remained relatively stagnant over the last month, with a particularly challenging week showing a 4.4% decline.
Despite having more room to recover than Bitcoin due to its deeper decline, Ethereum's lack of momentum raises questions about a potential rebound.
Bitcoin's biggest risk is a new decline that could reverse its gains and push its drawdown beyond 33.9%.
Investors should watch its September 14 starting price of $78,175, about 6.1% lower than its current level; falling below this threshold could weaken its appeal.
However, choosing Bitcoin could mean missing out on potentially larger gains, particularly if Ethereum rebounds and fuels faster growth in Arbitrum.
If Arbitrum can generate substantial fee revenue for its token holders, ARB could significantly outperform Bitcoin.
Arbitrum operates as a layer 2 solution, meaning it processes transactions on its own network and posts the results back to Ethereum for final validation.
This design allows Arbitrum to benefit from Ethereum's security while providing faster and cheaper transactions.
Users swapping tokens on Arbitrum pay significantly less than on Ethereum.
However, the relationship between the network's earning potential and the value ARB token holders gain remains unclear.
Bitcoin stands out as the largest asset among the three, holding a market capitalization of $1.67 trillion.
It has also experienced the least decline from its peak value, facing a drawdown of 33.9%.
Ethereum's stagnation poses a challenge for potential Arbitrum investors.
If Ethereum remains flat, Arbitrum may struggle to gain the same upward momentum.

He expects BTC to move back… Bitcoin slipped slightly below its two-hundred-week moving average before recovering, according to Michael Saylor, who says the market has begun turning upward. The Strategy executive told Bloomberg Television he believes the bull market is just beginning and expects Bitcoin to move back above $100,000. At the time of the report, BTC was trading at $83,761.77. Saylor said it had bounced from a low slightly below $60,000 and was moving into what he sees as more favorable conditions. “I think we hit the bottom around slightly below $60,000. I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said. His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support. Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset. “We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said. The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance. “I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction. Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares. He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors. Bitcoin slipped slightly below its two-hundred-week moving average before recovering, according to Michael Saylor, who says the market has begun turning upward. The Strategy executive told Bloomberg Television he believes the bull market is just beginning and expects Bitcoin to move back above $100,000.
At the time of the report, BTC was trading at $83,761.77. Saylor said it had bounced from a low slightly below $60,000 and was moving into what he sees as more favorable conditions.
“I think we hit the bottom around slightly below $60,000. I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said.

His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support.

Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset.
“We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said.

The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance.

“I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction.

Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares.

He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors.
Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total holdings to 848,250 BTC. The purchase was the company’s smallest Bitcoin buy in 2026.

For the week ended Oct. 9, Strategy sold 125,183 MSTR shares for $21 million and used the proceeds, along with $500 million from its USD Cash reserves, to fund its Bitcoin purchase. The company also repurchased 1.9 million STRC shares for $192.4 million.

Investor sentiment on Stocktwits was weak: retail sentiment around MSTR fell from “bearish” to “extremely bearish” over 24 hours amid low message volumes, while sentiment around BTC was “bearish,” also with low message volumes.

He expects BTC to move back… Bitcoin slipped slightly below its two-hundred-week moving average before recovering, according to Michael Saylor, who says the market has begun turning upward. The Strategy executive told Bloomberg Television he believes the bull market is just beginning and expects Bitcoin to move back above $100,000. At the time of the report, BTC was trading at $83,761.77. Saylor said it had bounced from a low slightly below $60,000 and was moving into what he sees as more favorable conditions. “I think we hit the bottom around slightly below $60,000. I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said. His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support. Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset. “We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said. The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance. “I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction. Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares. He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors. Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total holdings to 848,250 BTC. The purchase was the company’s smallest Bitcoin buy in 2026. For the week ended Oct. 9, Strategy sold 125,183 MSTR shares for $21 million and used the proceeds, along with $500 million from its USD Cash reserves, to fund its Bitcoin purchase. The company also repurchased 1.9 million STRC shares for $192.4 million. Investor sentiment on Stocktwits was weak: retail sentiment around MSTR fell from “bearish” to “extremely bearish” over 24 hours amid low message volumes, while sentiment around BTC was “bearish,” also with low message volumes. Bitcoin slipped slightly below its two-hundred-week moving average before recovering, according to Michael Saylor, who says the market has begun turning upward. The Strategy executive told Bloomberg Television he believes the bull market is just beginning and expects Bitcoin to move back above $100,000.
At the time of the report, BTC was trading at $83,761.77. Saylor said it had bounced from a low slightly below $60,000 and was moving into what he sees as more favorable conditions.
“I think we hit the bottom around slightly below $60,000. I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said.

His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support.

Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset.
“We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said.

The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance.

“I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction.

Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares.

He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors.
Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total holdings to 848,250 BTC. The purchase was the company’s smallest Bitcoin buy in 2026.

For the week ended Oct. 9, Strategy sold 125,183 MSTR shares for $21 million and used the proceeds, along with $500 million from its USD Cash reserves, to fund its Bitcoin purchase. The company also repurchased 1.9 million STRC shares for $192.4 million.

Investor sentiment on Stocktwits was weak: retail sentiment around MSTR fell from “bearish” to “extremely bearish” over 24 hours amid low message volumes, while sentiment around BTC was “bearish,” also with low message volumes.

extraction.body: New Shadow AI Discovery™ capability, enhanced Aurora Security Assistant skills, and expanded integrations help organizations govern AI, accelerate investigations, and strengthen their security posture EDEN PRAIRIE, Minn., Oct. 14, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Arctic Wolf®, the cybersecurity and AI company, today announced at the 2026 Security Operations Summit new capabilities in the Aurora ® Superintelligence Platform that help organizations gain visibility into AI adoption, access security insights faster, and extend protection across customers' rapidly expanding attack surfaces. As AI adoption accelerates across the enterprise, organizations face a growing challenge that they cannot secure what they cannot see. Employees are rapidly embracing AI-powered tools, security teams are managing increasingly complex environments, and critical security information remains scattered across multiple platforms and applications. Without visibility, organizations can't effectively manage AI risk. As a result, security teams struggle to prioritize risk and take action. According to a report by the Cloud Security Alliance, 98% of organizations experienced unsanctioned AI use. To help customers address these challenges, Arctic Wolf is introducing Shadow AI Discovery, a new feature that is designed to uncover and inventory sanctioned or unknown AI tools in use across an organization. Additionally, the company is adding new Aurora Security Assistant capabilities, and expanded technology integrations that bring more data, intelligence, and visibility into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform. "Security teams are under pressure to move faster while managing more data, more threats, and more AI risk than ever before," said Nick Schneider, president and chief executive officer at Arctic Wolf. "Visibility is the foundation of security in the age of AI. The advancements we are introducing today of the Aurora Superintelligence Platform help customers understand how AI is being used across their environment so they can establish stronger management processes and act on insights in real time." Visibility into AI Activity Across the Environment AI adoption is happening faster than many organizations can inventory, manage, or assess risk. According to the SANS 2026 AI Survey , 63% of practitioners cite a lack of visibility into where AI models are being used and what information they may expose. Soon available to Aurora Managed Detection and Response® (MDR) customers, Shadow AI Discovery is designed to identify AI tools in use across network, identity, and endpoint telemetry to create an inventory of AI activity, enable classification as sanctioned or unknown, and highlight potential data exposure risks without requiring additional deployments. With a centralized inventory of AI usage, organizations can better identify unauthorized tools, measure AI adoption trends, and evaluate the effectiveness of governance policies over time. When gaps are identified, organizations can assign AI-focused training through Aurora Security Awareness and Training to teach employees AI best practices and reduce human risk. Advancing Aurora Security Assistant to Deliver Comprehensive Answers Across Risk, Exposure, and Operational Queries Arctic Wolf is also significantly enhancing Aurora Security Assistant, the natural language interface to the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, with new skills that provide greater access to insights across the Arctic Wolf portfolio. Customers can now get information from Aurora Exposure Management, Aurora Threat Intelligence, and their own Security Journey, helping them to investigate issues faster and prioritize with context, all through simple, natural language conversation. The new skills enable customers to ask questions about outstanding Security Posture In-Depth Review (SPiDR) findings and Security Journey actions, such as what requires attention, which reviews need a response, and what steps should be taken next. They can also quickly understand their current risk posture by identifying critical vulnerabilities, riskiest assets, and endpoints that failed recent vulnerability scans. Grounded in the Security Operations Graph of the Aurora Superintelligence Platform®, Aurora Security Assistant helps customers move from searching for information to taking action, providing self-service access to security insights, recommendations, and operational context in seconds. Expanded Integrations Extend Security Coverage Arctic Wolf is further expanding the Aurora Superintelligence Platform with multiple new technology integrations enabled by the platform's Open Data Pipeline, which converts raw telemetry from across a customer's attack surface into high-quality security signal. These integrations broaden the telemetry monitored by the Aurora Agentic SOC and extend detection and active response capabilities across customers' existing environments, so organizations enhance the value of the technologies they already use without replacing them. New coverage includes: Web Application Firewalls (WAFs): New Cloudflare and Imperva integrations enable detection and active response for threats targeting web applications and services, helping customers respond faster to malicious activity. Backup and Recovery: A new integration with Veeam brings backup and recovery intelligence into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, extending visibility into backup infrastructure that attackers increasingly target to disrupt recovery efforts. Medical Provider Applications: New integrations with Epic Systems EHR, Claroty xDome Healthcare, and Imprivata ITDR. Additional integrations: ExtraHop Reveal(x) 360, Datadog, Proofpoint Essentials, 1Password, Google Workspace, Trend Vision One Endpoint Security, Palo Alto Cortex, and Claroty xDome Industrial. Together, these integrations bring even more of the customers' security ecosystem into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them expand visibility, strengthen detection and response, and get more value from their existing technology investments. Media Contact Oliver Cowley Manager, Corporate Communications, Arctic Wolf PR@arcticwolf.com

Visibility into AI Activity Across the Environment

AI adoption is happening faster than many organizations can inventory, manage, or assess risk. According to the SANS 2026 AI Survey , 63% of practitioners cite a lack of visibility into where AI models are being used and what information they may expose.

Soon available to Aurora Managed Detection and Response® (MDR) customers, Shadow AI Discovery is designed to identify AI tools in use across network, identity, and endpoint telemetry to create an inventory of AI activity, enable classification as sanctioned or unknown, and highlight potential data exposure risks without requiring additional deployments.

With a centralized inventory of AI usage, organizations can better identify unauthorized tools, measure AI adoption trends, and evaluate the effectiveness of governance policies over time. The new skills enable customers to ask questions about outstanding Security Posture In-Depth Review (SPiDR) findings and Security Journey actions, such as what requires attention, which reviews need a response, and what steps should be taken next. They can also quickly understand their current risk posture by identifying critical vulnerabilities, riskiest assets, and endpoints that failed recent vulnerability scans.

Grounded in the Security Operations Graph of the Aurora Superintelligence Platform®, Aurora Security Assistant helps customers move from searching for information to taking action, providing self-service access to security insights, recommendations, and operational context in seconds.

Arctic Wolf is further expanding the Aurora Superintelligence Platform with multiple new technology integrations enabled by the platform's Open Data Pipeline, which converts raw telemetry from across a customer's attack surface into high-quality security signal. These integrations broaden the telemetry monitored by the Aurora Agentic SOC and extend detection and active response capabilities across customers' existing environments, so organizations enhance the value of the technologies they already use without replacing them. New coverage includes:

Web Application Firewalls (WAFs): New Cloudflare and Imperva integrations enable detection and active response for threats targeting web applications and services, helping customers respond faster to malicious activity.

Backup and Recovery: A new integration with Veeam brings backup and recovery intelligence into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, extending visibility into backup infrastructure that attackers increasingly target to disrupt recovery efforts.
Medical Provider Applications: New integrations with Epic Systems EHR, Claroty xDome Healthcare, and Imprivata ITDR.
Additional integrations: ExtraHop Reveal(x) 360, Datadog, Proofpoint Essentials, 1Password, Google Workspace, Trend Vision One Endpoint Security, Palo Alto Cortex, and Claroty xDome Industrial.

Together, these integrations bring even more of the customers' security ecosystem into the Aurora Superintelligence Platform, helping them expand visibility, strengthen detection and response, and get more value from their existing technology investments.

Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection leverages AI-driven, intent-based detection designed to disrupt attacks mid-flight and advance a new era of preemptive cybersecurity EDEN PRAIRIE, Minn. – October 14, 2026 – Arctic Wolf®, the cybersecurity and AI company, today at its 2026 Security Operations Summit introduced Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection, a next-generation endpoint security solution designed to unlock AI-powered, intent-based detection to identify, disrupt, and reverse ransomware, credential theft, and other evasive attacks earlier in the attack chain. Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection introduces a new approach to endpoint security built for today’s AI threat landscape. As AI enables attackers to move faster and shorten the time to exploit, organizations need a solution that is designed to disrupt threats preemptively before malicious activity becomes visible by traditional security tools. Gartner® recently noted, “to stay ahead of AI-augmented attacks, enterprises are increasingly moving beyond reactive monitoring toward preemptive controls, specifically capabilities that can deny, deceive, and disrupt adversaries.” 1 Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection helps organizations make that shift by identifying malicious intent earlier in the attack lifecycle and helping stop attacks before they cause significant damage. Designed to operate alongside existing endpoint protection (EPP) and detection solutions (EDR), including third-party platforms and Aurora Endpoint Security, it extends protection without requiring organizations to replace what they already have. Rather than relying on individual indicators of compromise, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection predicts, maps, and analyzes endpoint activity to understand how processes and events unfold across the endpoint, enabling it to recognize when seemingly legitimate actions begin to converge toward a malicious outcome. By detecting intent earlier in the attack chain, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection can interrupt and roll back attacks before they fully materialize to help organizations address threats earlier than traditional EPP and EDR alone. Many of today’s attacks no longer rely on malware, making them harder to detect with conventional security tools. Instead, attackers leverage compromised credentials, trusted tools, and low-and-slow techniques that blend into normal business operations. The trend is accelerating, with ransomware accounting for 44% of Arctic Wolf incident response engagements in the last year. Credential theft continues to surge, with credential-harvesting malware collecting an estimated 1.7 billion credentials from 7.4 million infected devices. 2 As attackers increasingly use AI to automate reconnaissance, accelerate intrusion activity, and scale campaigns, security teams need new ways to identify threats earlier in the attack lifecycle. “Attackers often don’t need malware to cause damage. They can use legitimate tools, trusted credentials, and AI-driven automation to hide in plain sight, all at machine speed,” said Dan Schiappa, President of Technology and Services at Arctic Wolf. “That’s why endpoint security needs to evolve. Endpoint detection and response does rich detection well, but that work needs to happen earlier. Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection shifts the mindset from a purely detection and response approach to a more preemptive approach, identifying malicious intent and disrupting threats earlier in the attack chain.” Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection builds and analyzes a causal graph of endpoint activity across processes, files, registries, and API calls. By maintaining context over time, the solution understands how events are connected and can identify attacker intent even when individual actions appear benign. This enables earlier threat detection, interruption of malicious activity in progress, and prevention of attacks before they advance deeper into the environment. Leveraging advanced agentic workflows, including a custom-trained small language model, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection evaluates how endpoint activity unfolds to distinguish legitimate business operations from emerging threats. When malicious intent is confirmed, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection automatically interrupts the activity and reverses the entire attack chain, helping organizations recover faster while reducing manual remediation efforts. Key Capabilities of Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection: Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is backed by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform , which processes more than 10 trillion security events each week across more than 11,000 customers. By combining AI-driven analysis with Arctic Wolf’s AI-native security operations platform, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection delivers earlier threat detection, disruption, and recovery that complements existing endpoint solutions, while advancing the company’s approach for delivering Agentic-led security outcomes with human oversight and validation. Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is now available in an exclusive beta for Arctic Wolf customers. Organizations interested in participating can enroll beginning today. Aurora® Adaptive Threat Protection leverages AI-driven, intent-based detection designed to disrupt attacks mid-flight and advance a new era of preemptive cybersecurity

EDEN PRAIRIE, Minn. – October 14, 2026 – Arctic Wolf®, the cybersecurity and AI company, today at its 2026 Security Operations Summit introduced Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection, a next-generation endpoint security solution designed to unlock AI-powered, intent-based detection to identify, disrupt, and reverse ransomware, credential theft, and other evasive attacks earlier in the attack chain.

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection introduces a new approach to endpoint security built for today’s AI threat landscape. As AI enables attackers to move faster and shorten the time to exploit, organizations need a solution that is designed to disrupt threats preemptively before malicious activity becomes visible by traditional security tools. Gartner® recently noted, “to stay ahead of AI-augmented attacks, enterprises are increasingly moving beyond reactive monitoring toward preemptive controls, specifically capabilities that can deny, deceive, and disrupt adversaries.” 1

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection helps organizations make that shift by identifying malicious intent earlier in the attack lifecycle and helping stop attacks before they cause significant damage. Designed to operate alongside existing endpoint protection (EPP) and detection solutions (EDR), including third-party platforms and Aurora Endpoint Security, it extends protection without requiring organizations to replace what they already have.

Rather than relying on individual indicators of compromise, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection predicts, maps, and analyzes endpoint activity to understand how processes and events unfold across the endpoint, enabling it to recognize when seemingly legitimate actions begin to converge toward a malicious outcome. By detecting intent earlier in the attack chain, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection can interrupt and roll back attacks before they fully materialize to help organizations address threats earlier than traditional EPP and EDR alone.

Many of today’s attacks no longer rely on malware, making them harder to detect with conventional security tools. Instead, attackers leverage compromised credentials, trusted tools, and low-and-slow techniques that blend into normal business operations. The trend is accelerating, with ransomware accounting for 44% of Arctic Wolf incident response engagements in the last year. Credential theft continues to surge, with credential-harvesting malware collecting an estimated 1.7 billion credentials from 7.4 million infected devices. 2 As attackers increasingly use AI to automate reconnaissance, accelerate intrusion activity, and scale campaigns, security teams need new ways to identify threats earlier in the attack lifecycle.

“Attackers often don’t need malware to cause damage. They can use legitimate tools, trusted credentials, and AI-driven automation to hide in plain sight, all at machine speed,” said Dan Schiappa, President of Technology and Services at Arctic Wolf. “That’s why endpoint security needs to evolve. Endpoint detection and response does rich detection well, but that work needs to happen earlier. Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection shifts the mindset from a purely detection and response approach to a more preemptive approach, identifying malicious intent and disrupting threats earlier in the attack chain.”

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection builds and analyzes a causal graph of endpoint activity across processes, files, registries, and API calls. By maintaining context over time, the solution understands how events are connected and can identify attacker intent even when individual actions appear benign. This enables earlier threat detection, interruption of malicious activity in progress, and prevention of attacks before they advance deeper into the environment.

Leveraging advanced agentic workflows, including a custom-trained small language model, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection evaluates how endpoint activity unfolds to distinguish legitimate business operations from emerging threats. When malicious intent is confirmed, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection automatically interrupts the activity and reverses the entire attack chain, helping organizations recover faster while reducing manual remediation efforts.
Key Capabilities of Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection:

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is backed by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform , which processes more than 10 trillion security events each week across more than 11,000 customers. By combining AI-driven analysis with Arctic Wolf’s AI-native security operations platform, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection delivers earlier threat detection, disruption, and recovery that complements existing endpoint solutions, while advancing the company’s approach for delivering Agentic-led security outcomes with human oversight and validation.
Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is now available in an exclusive beta for Arctic Wolf customers. Organizations interested in participating can enroll beginning today.
Manager, Corporate Communications, Arctic Wolf

Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection introduces a new approach to endpoint security built for today’s AI threat landscape. As AI enables attackers to move faster and shorten the time to exploit, organizations need a solution that is designed to disrupt threats preemptively before malicious activity becomes visible by traditional security tools. Gartner® recently noted, “to stay ahead of AI-augmented attacks, enterprises are increasingly moving beyond reactive monitoring toward preemptive controls, specifically capabilities that can deny, deceive, and disrupt adversaries.” 1 Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection helps organizations make that shift by identifying malicious intent earlier in the attack lifecycle and helping stop attacks before they cause significant damage. Designed to operate alongside existing endpoint protection (EPP) and detection solutions (EDR), including third-party platforms and Aurora Endpoint Security, it extends protection without requiring organizations to replace what they already have. Rather than relying on individual indicators of compromise, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection predicts, maps, and analyzes endpoint activity to understand how processes and events unfold across the endpoint, enabling it to recognize when seemingly legitimate actions begin to converge toward a malicious outcome. By detecting intent earlier in the attack chain, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection can interrupt and roll back attacks before they fully materialize to help organizations address threats earlier than traditional EPP and EDR alone. Many of today’s attacks no longer rely on malware, making them harder to detect with conventional security tools. Instead, attackers leverage compromised credentials, trusted tools, and low-and-slow techniques that blend into normal business operations. The trend is accelerating, with ransomware accounting for 44% of Arctic Wolf incident response engagements in the last year. Credential theft continues to surge, with credential-harvesting malware collecting an estimated 1.7 billion credentials from 7.4 million infected devices. 2 As attackers increasingly use AI to automate reconnaissance, accelerate intrusion activity, and scale campaigns, security teams need new ways to identify threats earlier in the attack lifecycle. “Attackers often don’t need malware to cause damage. They can use legitimate tools, trusted credentials, and AI-driven automation to hide in plain sight, all at machine speed,” said Dan Schiappa, President of Technology and Services at Arctic Wolf. “That’s why endpoint security needs to evolve. Endpoint detection and response does rich detection well, but that work needs to happen earlier. Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection shifts the mindset from a purely detection and response approach to a more preemptive approach, identifying malicious intent and disrupting threats earlier in the attack chain.” Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection builds and analyzes a causal graph of endpoint activity across processes, files, registries, and API calls. By maintaining context over time, the solution understands how events are connected and can identify attacker intent even when individual actions appear benign. This enables earlier threat detection, interruption of malicious activity in progress, and prevention of attacks before they advance deeper into the environment. Leveraging advanced agentic workflows, including a custom-trained small language model, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection evaluates how endpoint activity unfolds to distinguish legitimate business operations from emerging threats. When malicious intent is confirmed, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection automatically interrupts the activity and reverses the entire attack chain, helping organizations recover faster while reducing manual remediation efforts. Key Capabilities of Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection: Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is backed by the Aurora Superintelligence Platform , which processes more than 10 trillion security events each week across more than 11,000 customers. By combining AI-driven analysis with Arctic Wolf’s AI-native security operations platform, Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection delivers earlier threat detection, disruption, and recovery that complements existing endpoint solutions, while advancing the company’s approach for delivering Agentic-led security outcomes with human oversight and validation. Aurora Adaptive Threat Protection is now available in an exclusive beta for Arctic Wolf customers. Organizations interested in participating can enroll beginning today. sources.title: Intel vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? - Yahoo Finance
passages: The semiconductor landscape is shifting as artificial intelligence demands new hardware.
Deciding between a turnaround giant like Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) and a networking specialist like Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) requires looking at their 2026 trajectories.
Erin Kennedy has no position in any of the stocks mentioned.
The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Advanced Micro Devices, Applied Materials, Broadcom, Intel, Marvell Technology, and Nvidia.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Marvell Technology focuses on data infrastructure, providing networking and storage solutions that power modern cloud and carrier environments.
The company has aggressively expanded its AI portfolio through the recent acquisitions of Celestial AI and Polariton Technologies.
Like its peers, Marvell faces significant concentration, with its 10 largest customers representing roughly 82% of total revenue and two specific customers each accounting for more than 10% of sales.
The balance sheet shows a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.3 as of January 2026.
Its current ratio of 2 suggests a healthy cushion to cover short-term obligations.
Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since this is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
It's not in the middle of overhauling its business.
The company faces customer concentration, but not on the same level as Intel.
Marvell's forward P/E is marginally less expensive.
And perhaps most importantly, Marvell is growing, and Intel is not.
The former's revenue surged more than 40% in its most recent fiscal year, and it flipped from reporting a loss to a healthy profit.
There are too many uncertainties tied to Intel's business makeover.
Intel is pivoting toward becoming a world-class foundry while maintaining its CPU dominance.
Marvell focuses on the plumbing of the data center, providing the high-speed connectivity needed for modern AI clusters.
Both companies compete for space in the global infrastructure market, but they offer distinct financial profiles for investors.
31, 2026, revenue reached approximately $8.2 billion, a significant 42.1% increase over the prior year.
Net income for the period was close to $2.7 billion, yielding a net margin of 32.6%.
This margin reflects the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses are paid, showing a sharp recovery from the net loss reported in its previous annual report.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.
*Stock Advisor returns as of October 14, 2026.
Intel designs and manufactures x86 processors while scaling Intel Foundry to offer advanced packaging and design enablement to the broader industry.
The company is leaning into its manufacturing strength through a deepened partnership with Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) for next-generation equipment.
Intel continues to be a central player among semiconductor stocks as it expands its foundry business.
Rapid advancements in AI could disrupt its business model if the company fails to keep pace with competitors or if customers choose to design chips internally.
Furthermore, Intel's reliance on third-party partners in Taiwan for certain manufacturing stages creates geographic risks related to political instability and global supply chain tensions.
It's pivoting toward providing chip manufacturing services for third parties.
In other words, the chipmaker is having to shell out quite a lot of money in order to build fabrication plants.
That spending will likely continue, as turning around a ship of Intel's size is neither a fast nor an easy endeavor.
The U.S. government's investment in Intel also gives me pause.
Before you buy stock in Intel, consider this:

sources.title: Floqer’s AI agents research sales prospects so teams don’t have to
passages: Floqer describes the technology as a fleet of AI agents that continuously research companies, people, and customer interactions, so team members don’t have to perform that work manually.
According to the company, customers have reported cutting prospecting time by as much as 70%.
Floqer’s first product looked nothing like its current one.
“We started with a Chrome extension, which is called ‘Super Chat,’” Mahajan told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this month.
“Anybody can go and log in with their ChatGPT account and then understand [information] and take notes.”
Floqer is pitching Wednesday on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 .
The startup told TechCrunch ahead of the presentation that it plans to open-source the technology behind its autonomous customer knowledge database.
It’s targeting early 2027 for the release, pending security reviews.
“So that was insightful for us, and then we pivoted from there to build Floqer.”

Floqer was founded in 2024 and has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding, with participation from investors such as Perplexity’s F7 Fund, N49P, Tidal Venture Partners, and Perplexity co-founder Denis Yarats.
It says it now has eight employees and more than 1,000 customers, including Perplexity, Wise, and AngelList.
Floqer aims to automate much of that research.
Users can describe what they are looking for, and its AI agents search across different sources to build lists of relevant companies and contacts.
The system also continuously monitors the web for changes.
If a prospect changes jobs, gets promoted, or works at a company that raises new funding, those updates can be reflected in the user’s customer records.
The company says its system can enrich accounts, or add detail about the companies a sales team is targeting, using more than 100 third-party data sources.
When it needs a verified email address or phone number, Floqer uses a “waterfall” approach, checking one data provider after another until it finds usable information.
The problem Floqer is trying to solve is familiar to anyone who has worked in sales or revenue operations.

Finding potential customers takes hours of searching Google, LinkedIn, company websites, job boards, and other sources to identify companies that fit a particular profile, then tracking down the right people and their contact information.
The decision comes partly in response to customer demand.
Mahajan said some companies want to host their own data rather than keep it inside a vendor’s proprietary platform.
Others want to modify the technology or build on top of it.
Before releasing the database publicly, Floqer is conducting security reviews because the database can contain sensitive customer information and large companies already use it.

extraction.body: WhatsApp’s new guest calling feature allows you to invite anyone to a call, without needing them to make an account first. They won’t need the app, either, since Meta also added support for calls on the web version of WhatsApp earlier this year. You can invite guests just by sending them the call link, and guests still have access to call features like hand raising, screen sharing, and emoji reactions, complete with end-to-end encryption. However, you still need an account to start a call, and there are a few restrictions for guests: > Anyone joining as a guest always needs the call host’s approval. Guests will enter a waiting room until the host lets them in and guests can be removed from the call at any time. Guests can’t see other participants’ phone numbers, send messages, or add anyone else directly to the call. Meta also says it’s launching Google and Outlook calendar integrations for WhatsApp calls later this year. After installing a WhatsApp plugin and connecting your account, you’ll be able to send a WhatsApp call link with your calendar invites.

sources.title: Ukraine blindsided by Starlink throttling restrictions and intelligence gaps
passages: Some Ukrainian officials speculated that SpaceX, which operated Starlink and the many thousands of terminals used in Ukraine by its military and civilians, introduced the restrictions at the request of the Trump administration after Musk posted messages critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week.

Ukrainian defense ministry adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said long-range drone operations were also impacted, as was Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russia’s new jet-powered drones, since Starlink is used on the interceptors being developed to combat them.
“It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation,” he wrote on Telegram.
The low speed presented several problems, including difficulties during drone take-offs and making them vulnerable to Russian air defenses.
“Slower targets become more vulnerable to enemy strikes,” the unit also noted.
It said “some missions had to be cancelled” due to the Starlink restrictions.
The president said there was “significant damage to facilities and equipment” at 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four in the oil and gas sector.
